about.title: Belvedere Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Belvedere is a small place, roughly 2,121 residents on a Marin County peninsula, and much of the ground people walk on here is steep, shared, or privately maintained. Think hillside steps, waterfront docks, sloped driveways, and the paths and lanes near Beach Road, Bayview Avenue, Graham Avenue and Peninsula Road. When a surface is slick, uneven, poorly lit, or missing a handrail and someone goes down, California premises liability law asks one central question: did the owner know about the hazard, or should they have known, and did they fail to fix it or warn people? That element, called notice, is where these cases are won or lost. It is also why same-day photos, the names of anyone who saw you fall, and a quick written request to preserve surveillance footage carry so much weight. You generally have two years to file, and considerably less if a public entity owns the property. LawProactive is a free connection service, not a law firm. Describe what happened and we will pair you with an independent attorney who takes premises cases on contingency.

whyChoose.title: Why Belvedere Residents Turn to LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice Is the Whole Case
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys we connect you with know how to build that proof through maintenance records, prior complaints and inspection logs.

items.title: Deadlines Differ by Owner
items.desc: Most premises claims carry a two-year filing window, but a fall on city, county or state property triggers a much shorter government claim deadline. Getting connected early keeps those options open.

items.title: Shared Blame Does Not End a Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, being partly responsible reduces your recovery rather than eliminating it. Preserving video and documenting the scene helps keep your share of fault where it belongs.

items.question: I fell on a public stairway or path in Belvedere. Is the deadline still two years?
items.answer: Probably not. If the City of Belvedere, Marin County or another public entity owns or maintains the spot where you fell, California generally requires a formal government claim within six months, well before the usual two-year limit. Because ownership of hillside lanes and waterfront access points is not always obvious, an attorney will typically confirm who controls the property right away.

items.question: What should I do in the first few days after a slip and fall?
items.answer: Get medical care first, even if the pain seems minor. Then photograph the hazard, your footwear and any lighting or signage, and write down what you remember while it is fresh. Ask the property owner or manager in writing to preserve any surveillance video, since many systems overwrite footage within days.
